question: What are the six constraints of REST architecture?
title: The Six REST Constraints
direct_answer: REST has six constraints: Client-Server, Stateless, Cacheable, Uniform Interface, Layered System, and Code-On-Demand (optional). Together they define what makes a system truly RESTful.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know REST beyond just HTTP verbs and understand the architectural principles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing only 2-3 constraints or confusing REST with HTTP
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how each constraint contributes to scalability and maintainability

sections.title: REST Architectural Constraints
sections.content: Roy Fielding defined REST in his 2000 dissertation with six architectural constraints. These aren't just guidelines—they define the REST architectural style. An API that violates these constraints isn't truly RESTful, even if it uses HTTP and JSON.

sections.title: The Six Constraints
content: 1. Client-Server: Separation of concerns — UI and data storage evolve independently
2. Stateless: Each request contains all information needed; server stores no client session state
3. Cacheable: Responses must define themselves as cacheable or non-cacheable (Cache-Control headers)
4. Uniform Interface: Standardized way to interact — resources, HTTP methods, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS
5. Layered System: Client cannot tell if it's connected directly to the server or through intermediaries (load balancers, caches, gateways)
6. Code-On-Demand (optional): Servers can extend client functionality by sending executable code (JavaScript)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: REST has six architectural constraints defined by Roy Fielding. The most critical ones are: Stateless, meaning each request is self-contained; Uniform Interface, which gives REST its predictability; and Layered System, which enables scalability through load balancers and caches. The others are Client-Server separation, Cacheability, and the optional Code-On-Demand. In practice, most REST APIs focus heavily on statelessness and uniform interface—those are what interviewers typically probe.

followup_questions: Which constraint do you think is most important and why?
What is HATEOAS and why is it rarely implemented?
How does statelessness affect horizontal scaling?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: REST isn't just HTTP plus JSON — it's an architectural style with six constraints. Know all six and you separate yourself from candidates who only know the verbs.

beats.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation. It's a set of six constraints — and an API is only truly RESTful when it follows them. The constraints aren't arbitrary rules; each one provides a specific architectural benefit.

Fielding needed a set of properties that would make distributed hypermedia systems scalable, reliable, and evolvable. The six constraints are the minimal set that achieves those goals over a standard HTTP network.

items: Client-Server: UI and data storage evolve independently — frontend and backend can change without breaking each other
Stateless: no server-side session; each request carries all needed context — enables horizontal scaling
Cacheable: responses must declare whether they can be cached — reduces server load and latency
Uniform Interface: standardized interaction model (URI resources, HTTP verbs, JSON representations) — makes every REST API predictable
Layered System: client cannot tell if it's talking to the origin server or an intermediary (load balancer, CDN, gateway) — enables transparent infrastructure
Code-On-Demand (optional): server can extend client functionality by sending executable code (e.g., JavaScript) — rarely used

beats.text: Our todo API satisfies all five mandatory constraints: the React frontend is separate (client-server), each request carries a JWT (stateless), GET /todos uses Cache-Control headers (cacheable), URIs are nouns and HTTP methods are verbs (uniform interface), and a load balancer sits in front of our Spring Boot instances without the client knowing (layered system). Code-on-demand doesn't apply here — we don't send JavaScript from the server. candidates miss: many freshers list only stateless and uniform interface. Listing all six — especially layered system and cacheability — signals that you've actually read about REST architecture, not just built APIs.

items: Listing only 2-3 constraints — interviewers asking this question expect all six; missing them signals shallow knowledge
Confusing REST constraints with application code layers (controller/service/repository) — layered system refers to network topology, not code structure

speakable_v2.cap: Six constraints: Client-Server, Stateless, Cacheable, Uniform Interface, Layered System, Code-On-Demand (optional). Stateless and Uniform Interface are the ones most probed in interviews.
followup_handoff: Why is statelessness the most important constraint for horizontal scaling?

question: Why is statelessness the most important REST constraint for scalability?
title: Statelessness and Scalability
direct_answer: Statelessness means the server stores no session data between requests. Every request carries its own authentication and context. This allows any server instance to handle any request, enabling horizontal scaling without sticky sessions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the real-world implications of REST constraints, not just memorization
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying stateless means the API has no state at all — the state lives in the client or database, not the server memory
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to JWT tokens and load balancing in Spring Boot

sections.title: Why Statelessness Enables Scaling
sections.content: In a stateful architecture, the server remembers who you are between requests using server-side sessions (HttpSession). This means you must always hit the same server — called sticky sessions. With statelessness, authentication info travels with every request (via JWT, API key, or OAuth token), so any server in a cluster can handle the request.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Stateful: server stores session → must use sticky sessions or shared session store (Redis)
Stateless: client sends JWT/token with every request → any server can handle it
Load balancer can freely route requests to any instance
Server restarts don't invalidate sessions
Tradeoff: slightly larger requests (token overhead), server can't easily invalidate sessions without a token blacklist

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Statelessness is key for scalability because it removes server-side session storage. When the server doesn't remember anything between requests, you can add more servers freely — a load balancer can route any request to any instance. In Spring Boot REST APIs, we achieve this with JWT tokens: the client sends the JWT in every Authorization header, so no server memory is needed. The tradeoff is that logout is harder since you can't just delete a server-side session — you need a token blacklist or short expiry times.

followup_questions: How do you handle logout in a stateless JWT-based system?
When would you choose stateful sessions over JWT?

seo.metaTitle: REST Statelessness and Scalability | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Understand why statelessness matters for REST API scalability. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Statelessness is the constraint that makes horizontal scaling cheap — no shared session means any server can handle any request.

beats.text: Statelessness means the HTTP server layer holds zero per-client state between requests. Every request must carry all the information needed to process it — including authentication. The server treats each request as if it has never seen this client before.

When servers hold session state, a load balancer must route each client to the same server every time — sticky sessions. That ties your infrastructure to individual servers. Remove session state, and any server in the pool handles any request. Scaling becomes adding more boxes.

items: JWT in Authorization header: carries the user's identity without a server-side lookup
SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS in Spring Security: prevents Spring from creating HttpSession
Horizontal scaling: a load balancer routes requests to any available server — no stickiness needed
Tradeoff: logout is harder — you can't invalidate a server-side session; use token blacklists or short expiry

beats.text: Todo app deployed on three servers behind a load balancer. User logs in, gets a JWT. Every request — GET /todos, POST /todos — includes Authorization: Bearer token. Server 1 handles the first request, server 3 handles the next — neither needs to know about the other. If server 2 crashes, its requests route to 1 and 3 seamlessly. Sharp edge: stateless does not mean the system has no state. The database is stateful. Your S3 bucket is stateful. Stateless means the HTTP application server doesn't hold per-client session memory between calls.

items: Saying stateless means no state at all — the state lives in the database and client; stateless refers to the HTTP server layer only
Storing user context in HttpSession in a Spring REST controller — that creates statefulness and forces sticky sessions

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless = no server session. JWT in every request. Any server handles any call. Enables horizontal scaling. Tradeoff: logout requires a token blacklist.
followup_handoff: How do you handle logout in a stateless JWT-based system?

question: What is the Uniform Interface constraint and what are its four sub-constraints?
title: Uniform Interface Sub-Constraints
direct_answer: Uniform Interface means all REST APIs interact the same way. Its four sub-constraints are: resource identification in requests (URIs), manipulation of resources through representations (JSON/XML), self-descriptive messages (Content-Type headers), and HATEOAS (hypermedia links).

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of REST knowledge beyond surface-level understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing HATEOAS exists or confusing it with pagination links
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Acknowledge that HATEOAS is rarely implemented in practice and explain why

sections.title: Uniform Interface Explained
sections.content: The Uniform Interface is what makes REST predictable and standardized. It means regardless of which REST API you use, the interaction model is the same: use URIs to identify resources, use HTTP methods to act on them, exchange JSON/XML representations, and (ideally) include hypermedia links.

sections.title: Four Sub-Constraints
content: 1. Resource identification: URIs uniquely identify resources (/users/123)
2. Manipulation through representations: JSON or XML body, not the resource itself
3. Self-descriptive messages: Content-Type: application/json tells client how to parse
4. HATEOAS: Response includes links to related actions — rarely implemented in real APIs

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Uniform Interface constraint has four parts. First, resources are identified by URIs. Second, clients interact through representations — you send and receive JSON, not the actual database record. Third, messages are self-descriptive through headers like Content-Type. Fourth, there's HATEOAS — Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State — where responses include links to next possible actions. In practice, most APIs skip HATEOAS because it adds complexity without enough benefit for typical use cases.

followup_questions: What is HATEOAS and why don't most APIs implement it?
How does Content-Type negotiate between JSON and XML?

seo.metaTitle: REST Uniform Interface Constraint | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn the four sub-constraints of REST Uniform Interface including HATEOAS. Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Uniform Interface is what makes every REST API feel familiar — same rules, same patterns, whether it's Stripe or your own service.

beats.text: The Uniform Interface constraint means all REST APIs interact the same standardized way regardless of the domain. It's the constraint that gives REST its predictability. You can guess how a REST API works before reading its docs because the interface pattern is uniform.

If every API invented its own interaction model, every client would need custom knowledge. Uniform Interface standardizes the four elements of every REST interaction so any client can work with any server.

items: Resource identification: every resource has a URI that uniquely identifies it — /todos/42 always means todo 42
Manipulation through representations: clients exchange JSON (a representation of the resource), not the resource itself
Self-descriptive messages: Content-Type: application/json tells the receiver how to parse the body; Accept header tells the server what format the client wants
HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses include links to related actions — rarely implemented in practice because of added complexity

beats.text: Todo API: GET /todos/42 returns {id:42, title:Buy milk, done:false} with Content-Type: application/json. That response is a representation of todo 42 — not the database row, but a JSON view of it. A HATEOAS response would also include _links:{self:/todos/42, mark-done:{href:/todos/42, method:PATCH}}. In Spring Boot, the Spring HATEOAS library supports this, but most teams skip it. The other three sub-constraints are universally followed; HATEOAS is the one where real-world REST diverges from Fielding's ideal. non-obvious: HATEOAS is technically part of the Uniform Interface constraint — not a separate REST level. Roy Fielding has said APIs without HATEOAS aren't truly REST, but the industry has mostly moved on.

items: Not knowing HATEOAS exists — even if you don't use it, knowing it's the fourth sub-constraint shows depth
Confusing Uniform Interface (a REST constraint) with code architecture patterns like MVC

speakable_v2.cap: Uniform Interface = URI identification + JSON representations + self-descriptive messages + HATEOAS (optional in practice). First three are universal; HATEOAS is the ideal rarely reached.

question: What does the Layered System constraint mean and how does it enable enterprise architecture?
title: Layered System Constraint
direct_answer: Layered System means clients cannot tell whether they're communicating directly with the server or through intermediaries like load balancers, API gateways, or CDNs. Each layer only knows about the adjacent layer, enabling modularity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding how REST fits into real-world infrastructure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking this is just about code layers (controller/service/repo) rather than network topology
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples: API Gateway, CDN caching, load balancer, reverse proxy

sections.title: What Layered System Means
sections.content: The Layered System constraint says the client doesn't need to know if it's talking to the actual server or an intermediary. A request from a mobile app might pass through: DNS → CDN → Load Balancer → API Gateway → Application Server. The client just sends an HTTP request and gets a response.

sections.title: Common Intermediary Layers
content: CDN: Caches static responses geographically close to users
Load Balancer: Distributes traffic across multiple server instances
API Gateway: Rate limiting, authentication, routing (AWS API Gateway, Kong)
Reverse Proxy: Nginx or Apache in front of Spring Boot app
Benefit: Each layer can be added/changed without client knowing

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Layered System constraint means the client only knows it's sending HTTP requests — it doesn't need to know if there's a load balancer, CDN, or API gateway between it and the actual application server. In a typical Spring Boot production deployment, your mobile app hits CloudFront for caching, then an AWS load balancer, then an API Gateway for auth and rate limiting, and finally your Spring Boot instance. The REST client is unaware of all these layers.

followup_questions: What is an API Gateway and what does it do?
How does CDN caching work with REST APIs?
What's the difference between a reverse proxy and a load balancer?

seo.metaTitle: REST Layered System Constraint | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Understand the REST Layered System constraint and API gateway architecture. Java backend prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: The Layered System constraint is why you can put a CDN and an API gateway in front of your Spring Boot app without changing a line of client code.

beats.text: The Layered System constraint says a REST client cannot tell — and doesn't need to tell — whether it's communicating directly with the origin server or through intermediaries. Each layer only sees the adjacent layer. The client sends an HTTP request and gets a response; what happens in between is invisible.

This constraint makes infrastructure changes transparent to clients. You can add a CDN for caching, an API gateway for rate limiting, or a new load balancer without any client code change. Layers are independently modifiable.

items: Load balancer: distributes traffic across Spring Boot instances — client is unaware which instance responds
API gateway: handles rate limiting, authentication, and routing — client just calls one host
CDN (CloudFront/Cloudflare): caches GET responses geographically near users — client gets faster response without knowing about the cache
Reverse proxy (Nginx): terminates SSL, compresses responses — invisible to client

beats.text: Todo app in production: mobile client calls api.todoapp.com/todos. DNS resolves to CloudFront. CloudFront checks its cache — miss — forwards to AWS ALB. ALB routes to one of three Spring Boot pods. Spring Boot fetches from Postgres and responds. CloudFront caches the 200 response. Client got a response and has no idea about any of those hops. production trap: many freshers think 'layered system' refers to the controller/service/repository layers in their code. That's application architecture. The REST constraint is about network topology — the layers between the client and the origin server.

items: Thinking layered system means code layers (controller/service/repository) — it refers to network intermediaries, not application architecture
Not knowing any examples — load balancer, CDN, API gateway, reverse proxy are all concrete instances of this constraint in action

speakable_v2.cap: Layered System = client can't see network intermediaries. Load balancers, CDNs, API gateways are all transparent layers. Infrastructure evolves without breaking clients.
followup_handoff: What is an API gateway and what does it do?
How does CDN caching interact with REST cacheability?

question: What is cacheability in REST and how do you control it with HTTP headers?
title: REST Cacheability and Cache-Control Headers
direct_answer: The Cacheable constraint requires REST responses to explicitly state whether they can be cached. This is done via Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified headers. Caching reduces server load and improves response times.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding HTTP caching mechanics in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying REST APIs can't be cached because they're dynamic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Cache-Control directives and ETag for conditional requests

sections.title: REST Cacheability
sections.content: The Cacheable constraint means every REST response must be labeled as cacheable or not. GET requests for product listings or user profiles can be cached. POST/PUT/DELETE are typically not cached. Proper caching dramatically reduces database load and API latency.

sections.title: Cache Control Headers
content: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 — cache for 1 hour
Cache-Control: no-cache — always revalidate with server
Cache-Control: no-store — never cache (sensitive data)
ETag: server sends hash of response; client sends If-None-Match on next request
304 Not Modified: server says cache is still valid
In Spring Boot: ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(1, TimeUnit.HOURS)).body(data)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Cacheable constraint requires REST APIs to communicate caching intent through headers. For example, a product catalog endpoint might return Cache-Control: max-age=3600 to allow a 1-hour cache. For conditional caching, ETags let the client ask 'has this changed?' — if not, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth. In Spring Boot, you use the CacheControl builder in ResponseEntity to set these headers. Sensitive endpoints like user data should use Cache-Control: no-store.

followup_questions: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
How do ETags work for optimistic concurrency?

seo.metaTitle: REST Cacheability and HTTP Headers | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn REST cacheability constraint and Cache-Control headers in Spring Boot. Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: REST APIs absolutely can be cached — the cacheability constraint just requires you to declare your intent with the right headers.

beats.text: The Cacheable constraint says every REST response must indicate whether it can be cached or not. This is done through HTTP caching headers. When GET responses are cached correctly, browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies can serve them without hitting your server at all.

Caching is one of the main scalability levers in REST. If a product catalog can be cached for an hour, your Spring Boot app and database only get hit once every hour for that data instead of once per request. Without the constraint requiring explicit cache declarations, intermediaries can't know what's safe to cache.

items: Cache-Control: max-age=3600: client and CDN can cache this response for 1 hour
Cache-Control: no-cache: must revalidate with the server on every request (still may cache but validates)
Cache-Control: no-store: never cache — use for sensitive data like account details
ETag: server sends a hash of the response; client sends If-None-Match: hash on next request; server returns 304 if unchanged
304 Not Modified: response with no body — the cache is still valid, saving bandwidth

beats.text: Todo app: GET /todos is user-specific and changes frequently — use Cache-Control: no-cache so the client always validates. GET /api/categories (static list of categories) — use Cache-Control: max-age=86400 for a 24-hour cache. GET /users/me (account info) — use Cache-Control: no-store, private. In Spring Boot: ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(1, TimeUnit.HOURS)).body(data). For ETags, return the ResponseEntity with an ETag header and check If-None-Match in the request. non-obvious: many devs think REST APIs can't be cached because they return dynamic data. Dynamic data can still be cached — it's just cached for a shorter time. Even a 30-second cache on a high-traffic endpoint dramatically reduces DB load.

items: Saying REST APIs can't be cached because they're dynamic — even a 30-second max-age cuts DB hits dramatically on high-traffic endpoints
Not setting Cache-Control at all — without it, browsers and proxies make their own caching decisions, which may cache sensitive data or never cache safe data

speakable_v2.cap: Cacheable = REST responses must declare their cacheability. Cache-Control for duration, ETag for conditional validation, no-store for sensitive data. Caching is a REST scalability superpower.
